episodes.168835: Showers and isolated thunderstorms along the Atlantic coast sea breeze pushed inland toward the I-75 corridor Sunday afternoon. Strong to severe pulse storms developed when the Atlantic coast sea breeze interacted with outflows from the Gulf coast sea breeze over inland southeast Georgia and Suwannee Valley. The main hazard was gusty, wet downburst winds, locally heavy rainfall and hail.
episodes.168838: A lingering front was across SE GA and this boundary interacted with the diurnally enhanced sea breezes as a mid level short wave trough passed overhead to trigger scattered strong to severe storms across the area in the afternoon and early evening.

episodes.169470: Lake Erie and northern OH were within the warm sector during the afternoon and early evening of the 6th as a surface low drifted eastward from central Lake Michigan to central Lower MI. A stationary front extended eastward from the low to Lake Ontario, while the trailing cold front drifted southeastward from southern Lake Michigan toward southern Lower MI and northern IN. Multicell thunderstorms generated an isolated gale-force peak wind gust near Marblehead as the line of storms evolved generally eastward along the northwest OH shore during the early evening of the 6th. These storms occurred within a warm sector comprised of moderate to strong effective bulk shear, moderate MUCAPE, and weak to moderate DCAPE.
episodes.169815: Moist and unstable southwest flow moved into the region early on Sunday, June 5th. Favorable upper level dynamics combined with sufficient daytime heating led to several rounds of long-lasting severe thunderstorms through the overnight hours.
episodes.169820: Numerous severe thunderstorms developed across east-central Florida along the east coast sea breeze, and along the main sea breeze collision. These storms produced waterspouts in Volusia County, and severe wind gusts along the Space and Treasure Coasts.
episodes.169824: Numerous severe thunderstorms developed across east-central Florida along the east coast sea breeze, and along the main sea breeze collision. Then, as storms moved offshore they produced severe wind gusts along the coast in Brevard, Indian River, and Martin Counties. One storm produced an EF-0 tornado in Saint Lucie County west of Fort Pierce.

Some of the storms produced rainfall of 1 to 3 inches in a short period of time, leading to localized flash flooding.  The flooding was primarily focused along and north of an Abingdon to Lacon line.
episodes.170226: Severe thunderstorms developed over the Nebraska Panhandle late in the evening of the 5th into the early morning hours of the 6th. Gusty winds and up to half dollar sized hail was reported.
episodes.170330: A fairly localized burst of strong to severe thunderstorms impacted western portions of South Central Nebraska on this Sunday evening. Primarily between 7-9:30 p.m. CDT, a cluster of intense convection tracked southeastward across much of Dawson County and into Phelps County before weakening below severe limits. All known severe-criteria reports emanated from the Lexington area, including quarter to golf ball size hail and unofficial mesonet-measured wind gusts up to 68 MPH. In Phelps County, all storm reports were slightly sub-severe, including small hail and measured wind gusts up to 54 MPH. Storms were progressive enough to keep rain totals solidly under 2 inches, and there were no reports of notable flooding. ||Breaking down event evolution and meteorological background, it initially appeared that this event might have been more widespread/impactful than it ultimately was. However, a few rounds of earlier-day convection in the general region...one consisting of fairly widespread showers/non-severe storms across much of South Central Nebraska and another featuring localized severe storms/flooding in north central Kansas...teamed up to effectively disrupt/stabilize the environment across enough local counties to diminish the scope of evening convection. The first isolated, supercellular storms of the late afternoon actually fired up a bit northwest of the local area (within western/north central NE) and started tracking southeast. Just as storms started invading Dawson County around 7 p.m. CDT, consolidating outflows allowed convective mode to transition from discrete to more of a small-scale complex. Although Dawson was the only county in the local area with verified severe weather, for the second straight evening a severe storm narrowly missed western Furnas County...passing just to the west. Once the initial severe storm weakened over Phelps County around 9:30 p.m. CDT, the South Central Nebraska severe weather threat effectively ended for the night and the entire local area was storm-free by around midnight. In the mid-upper levels, this event was only modestly-forced, as the region resided under broad west-northwest flow containing various low amplitude disturbances, but with slightly stronger deep layer wind shear versus the preceding evening's round of severe storms (around 40 knots). There were no notable surface features in play, only a weak quasi-stationary front draped in west-east fashion across central NE. At the surface, afternoon temperatures in the Dawson County area topped out in the low 80s F with dewpoint averaging low-mid 60s, promoting decent mixed-layer CAPE of 1500-2000 J/kg as storms moved in.
episodes.170333: This Monday afternoon-evening featured the third consecutive day of severe thunderstorms within South Central Nebraska, this time highlighted by a few intense supercells that rolled southeastward through primarily central portions of the area, leaving behind fairly narrow (but in places significant) swaths of damaging winds and/or large hail. The first supercell of the day to invade the local area actually barely brushed its northeast edges, dropping out of northeast Nebraska and skirting eastern/northern portions of Nance, Merrick and Polk counties mainly 3:15-4:15 p.m. CDT before weakening. Although radar signatures and reports from just outside this coverage area suggested that larger hail likely occurred within a small part of South Central Nebraska (especially eastern Nance), the only ground-truth consisted of nickel size stones in Genoa. Following this early activity, a lull of a few hours ensued before the day's main event got underway, consisting of a closely knit pair of twin supercells (precipitation cores separated by no more than 10-15 miles) that marched in step through primarily the following counties between 7-9:30 p.m. CDT: northeastern Dawson, much of Buffalo, northeastern Phelps, much of Kearney, northern/eastern Franklin and western Webster (the separate storm cores eventually merged southeast of Minden). As for wind impacts along this corridor, a few of the most notable reports featured: estimated 100 MPH winds in the Minden area that took down three large metal transmission towers; a mesonet-measured gust of 79 MPH near Axtell and a garage destroyed in town; estimated 70 MPH gusts in the Elm Creek, Kearney and Campbell areas (Kearney Regional Airport AWOS peaked at 61 MPH). All along the aforementioned corridor, there were many instances of flipped irrigation pivots, broken power poles and damaged crops. Hail reports were limited during this main event, but size tended to prevail on the smaller to marginally-severe spectrum, including quarter size stones in Sumner, Odessa and Axtell. About an hour after this initial supercell cluster departed Webster County into Kansas, another large supercell took aim into eastern Dawson/western Buffalo counties from the northwest between 10:30-11:30 p.m. CDT, following a remarkably similar path as the earlier storms and yielding reports of quarter to golf ball size hail in the Eddyville and Miller area before weakening while approaching Interstate 80. A bit later this storm reintensified to radar-indicated severe levels in the Blue Hill area, but there were no verifying reports before it weakened for good over Nuckolls County by 1:30 a.m. CDT, ending the severe storm threat for the night. Outside of the aforementioned supercells, the only other South Central Nebraska severe weather report was a rogue 59 MPH wind gust in Edison, associated with the north end of an overall-weak convective complex that brushed through Furnas, Harlan and Franklin counties from the west between 9-11 p.m. CDT.||Turning to the meteorological background, all supercells that impacted South Central Nebraska initiated at least slightly, if not significantly off to the north-northwest before infiltrating the local area. In fact, the later-evening supercell that entered Dawson/Buffalo counties around 10:30 p.m. CDT developed and first became severe-warned some eight hours prior and 320 miles away...over Weston County, WY! Clearly, the mesoscale environment was quite supportive of long-lived supercells. From a big picture perspective, the basic mid-upper level situation over Nebraska had changed little versus the previous few days, continuing to feature persistent west-northwest flow. However, the big difference on the 6th was that this upper flow became noticeably stronger (aided by the arrival of a pronounced jet streak evident at 300 millibars). As a result, deep layer wind shear ramped up to as high as 50-60 knots. This strong shear profile more than compensated for seasonably-modest instability levels, with evening mixed-layer CAPE over South Central Nebraska only averaging 1000-1500 J/kg. At the surface, there were no features of note, only a weak frontal zone stretched across Nebraska in generally west-northwest to east-southeast fashion.
episodes.170382: A shortwave trough dropped out of the Canadian Rockies and across the upper midwest. Storms developed along a surface boundary in the afternoon, resulting in a few hail reports and a strong wind gust. In addition to the moderate CAPE , the backed wind profile supported some rotation within storms. While no tornadoes occurred there was a funnel cloud reported north of the Des Moines metro.  Later that night the deep warm cloud layer and high precipitable water values made for efficient rain producers. As storms continued overnight along a stationary boundary locally heavy rain resulted in flash flooding in central Iowa.
episodes.170383: A shortwave trough axis passed over the state and thunderstorms that had formed along a boundary in the early morning hours strengthened by midday. Despite relatively weak shear profiles, storms were able to organize enough to produce damaging wind gusts in Guthrie county. The storm complex continued into southeast Iowa into the afternoon, remaining below severe limits.||Rainfall in the Des Moines River basin was able to push the river, at Fleur Drive, briefly into flood stage on the 7th as well.
episodes.170538: A line of strong to severe thunderstorms moved through eastern Oklahoma during the early morning hours of the 6th. The strongest storms produced damaging wind gusts.
episodes.170550: Multiple rounds of thunderstorms affected northeastern Oklahoma and southeastern Kansas on the 5th through the morning of the 6th. The Grand-Neosho River basin received heavy rainfall from these thunderstorms, which resulted in moderate flooding of the Neosho River near Commerce.
episodes.170554: Severe thunderstorms produced large hail, which ranged from nickel to quarter size.
episodes.170589: Thunderstorms developed over Sheridan and western Cherry County during the afternoon hours of June 5th. Coverage of thunderstorms became more numerous as activity moved into the central Sandhills from northwestern Nebraska. As this activity tracked to the southeast, numerous reports of large hail and a brief tornado touch down was reported. Two inch diameter hail was reported in Callaway which broke several windows on residences.
episodes.170590: A persistent stationary front served as the focal point for thunderstorm development during the afternoon hours of June 6th. Thunderstorms developed over western Cherry and Sheridan county and tracked to the southeast, across the Sandhills into portions of central Nebraska. A brief tornado touch down was reported over far northwestern Cherry county. Hail up to golf ball size and thunderstorm wind gusts to 70 MPH were reported with the strongest storms.
episodes.170627: Storms produced a brief tornado into addition to numerous hail reports.
episodes.170915: A mesoscale convective system (MCS) moved through the Ozarks and into the Mid-South on the morning of June 6th. Numerous showers and thunderstorms moved across the Mid-South during the morning hours. This activity weakened and produced outflow boundaries. These boundaries interacted with an increasingly moist and unstable atmosphere and by early evening convection had redeveloped. This resulted in numerous showers and thunderstorms with heavy rainfall, damaging wind, and large hail.
episodes.170927: A complex of storms initially developed across central Kansas during the evening hours or June 5th, 2022. The storms initially produced damaging winds, flash flooding and large hail across central Kansas, before propagating to the south, producing damaging winds and flooding across south central Kansas during the late evening hours.
episodes.171003: High plains convection moved southeastward into northern Oklahoma late on the evening of the 5th into the 6th, with reports of large hail and severe wind gusts received.
episodes.171177: Two different thunderstorms moved south through Southwest Nebraska during the afternoon and into the evening hours.  Hail up to grapefruit size was reported near McCook.  The same storm produced wind gusts up to 64 MPH near Indianola.
episodes.171179: During the afternoon a thunderstorm formed near Bogue, producing hail up to golf ball size.  Later in the evening a thunderstorm moved south from Nebraska into Northwest Kansas.  Hail up to lime size was reported with this storm.
episodes.171191: A weak frontal boundary drifted into the region during the afternoon of the 2nd sparking scattered thunderstorms. The boundary lingered in the region for a few days causing thunderstorms through the 5th.
episodes.171421: Numerous strong to severe thunderstorms began to develop just north of the region mid-afternoon on June 5th. As the storms pushed southward they encountered much more unstable air, better moisture, and stronger shear, leading to several storms producing large damaging hail and wind gusts.
episodes.171431: Strong to severe storms developed along the foothills and Palmer Divide in eastern Colorado and moved south-southeast out across the plains. Storms quickly became severe moving off the higher terrain onto the warm and moist plains producing intense rainfall rates, flash flooding, and large damaging hail through the late evening hours.
episodes.171564: Another round widespread stratiform rain showers impacted the Inland Northwest. With the ground already saturated from previous system, the rain began to impact the region quickly with three quarters to an inch of rain.
episodes.171565: Another round widespread stratiform rain showers impacted the Inland Northwest. With the ground already saturated from previous system, the rain began to impact the region quickly with three quarters to an inch of rain.
episodes.171578: A typical summertime pattern prevailed with a few strong thunderstorms producing wind gusts in excess of 34 knots.
episodes.171671: Scattered showers and thunderstorms affected Middle Tennessee during the afternoon and evening hours on June 6. A few reports of large hail and wind damage were received.
episodes.171684: A MCS that pushed across northern zones produced severe weather. DCAPE values of around 1000 J/kg through this area with ample microburst potential. Another MCS complex developed into central Kansas in Ellis County pushing south into south central Kansas clipping the southeastern counties of the CWA. CAPE values near 1500 J/kg and shear values over 30kts helped to aid with instability in this area.
episodes.171687: Strong daytime heating through the afternoon coupled with ample low level convergence, there were many severe reports for hail early and and wind gusts later in the overnight. A shortwave trough helped to amplify this round of storms being more widespread but with greater moisture buoyancy further east. Shear was over 30 knots with the earlier more discreet cells, allowing for some large hail. DCAPE values associated with good outflows allowed for many 60 mph wind gusts and above later in the night.
episodes.171709: An upper level trough over the eastern Gulf of Mexico along with moist SW wind flow led to a prolonged period of major flooding in southern Miami-Dade County. Rainfall on Monday, June 6th and early Tuesday June 7th associated with a surge of moisture in the wake of the June 3-4 tropical disturbance led to localized very heavy rainfall of 5-8 inches in portions of South Miami-Dade County, aggravating pre-existing flooding and causing additional major flooding.
episodes.171751: An axis of instability was draped across much of the area during a multi-day stretch in June, which served as a catalyst for diurnally driven convection across portions of north and central Georgia. These storms and its respective outflows produced numerous reports of trees and powerlines down, with minor structural damage at some locations.

The Neosho River near Commerce rose above its flood stage of 15 feet at 5:00 pm CDT on June 6th. The river crested at 18.27 feet at 9:45 pm CDT on the 7th, resulting in moderate flooding. Riverview Park experienced moderate flooding, and low lying areas around Miami were cut off. The river fell below flood stage at 12:15 pm CDT on the 8th.

Based on pictures and videos received from Saint Lucie County Emergency management, trained spotters, local broadcast media, and the public, an EF-0 tornado impacted parts of north-central Saint Lucie County. Peak winds are estimated between 65-70 mph. The discontinuous tornado track began approximately 7 miles northwest of Lakewood Park, in a field north of Florida's Turnpike and west of Interstate 95 at approximately 1706LST. The tornado drifted slowly to the south and east, eventually moving across the Turnpike near mile marker 161 at approximately 1714LST. The tornado then tracked southeast where it damaged the roof of a barn, knocked down power lines, and tipped over a trailer at the 14500th block of West Angle Road at 1717LST. The tornado dissipated over a field shortly thereafter.
